summary: West Point Lighthouse, Prince Edward Island, first lit in May 1876; William MacDonald kept it for fifty years, and an inn has used the tower since 1984.

structures.note: Square tapered tower, frame construction on stone foundations, 67 ft 8 in ground to vane (HistoricPlaces; PEI Lighthouse Society).

access.note: Grounds and tower open; inn and museum on site (LighthouseFriends visiting notes).

stay.season: late May to early October (LighthouseFriends visiting notes)
stay.note: Guests can spend the night in the tower if booking far ahead (LighthouseFriends).

facts.agency: West Point Development Corporation (owner since 21 May 2002)

events.note: Construction began 1875 by Mugridge and Company of Shediac (LighthouseFriends; HistoricPlaces).
Revolving light first shown 21 May 1876; eight lamps and reflectors; one red flash and three white every 90 s.
William MacDonald appointed keeper; the 1902 statement gives 1 December 1875 (scan p.246, printed p.69). The Society gives 1875.
Red bands on the tower changed to black for visibility.
Benjamin MacIsaac replaced William MacDonald on 9 April 1925.
Light automated 19 May 1963 (LighthouseFriends); the PEI Lighthouse Society gives 29 May 1963. Keeper's dwelling torn down shortly after.
Leased to the West Point Development Corporation by the Canadian Coast Guard.
Dwelling rebuilt from original blueprints; opened 1 July 1984 as Canada's only Inn in a Lighthouse.
Ownership awarded to the West Point Development Corporation on 21 May 2002, first such transfer on PEI.
Recognised under the PEI Heritage Places Protection Act on 1 Nov 2012 (LighthouseFriends). The record gives 2011.
Inveresh, a square-rigged ship, wrecked on the West Point reef.
Norwegian ship Nandi grounded on the beach a mile or two north of the lighthouse in mid-November; neither ship nor crew injured; refloated the following spring.

keepers.name: William MacDonald
keepers.note: Known as "Lighthouse Willie". The 1902 keepers' statement reads "McDonald, Wm" / West Point / Dec. 1, 1875 (matched by position in the OCR; confirmed on the page image, scan p.246, printed p.69). The Society gives 1875. HistoricPlaces names him first keeper when the light became operational in May 1876. LighthouseFriends spells his wife's name Mariah; the Society has Maria.

keepers.name: Benjamin MacIsaac
keepers.note: Replaced MacDonald on 9 April 1925 (Society); First World War veteran; the light was automated on 19 May 1963 (LighthouseFriends).

corrections.why: HistoricPlaces and the PEI Lighthouse Society both give 67 ft 8 in (20.6 m) from ground to vane. The record's 20.0 m is not supported by either; 20.1 m is the focal height.

corrections.proposed: West Point Development Corporation, owner since 21 May 2002
corrections.why: LighthouseFriends and the PEI Lighthouse Society both record the 2002 transfer from the federal government.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends and HistoricPlaces date the start of construction to 1875 and operation to May 1876; the record's 1876 is the year the light was first shown.
The record's 'ownership unknown' conflicts with the 2002 transfer recorded by both LighthouseFriends and the PEI Lighthouse Society; see corrections.
LighthouseFriends gives 19 May 1963 for automation; the PEI Lighthouse Society gives 29 May 1963. Not resolved; the story states both.

notes_for_editor:
1. Heritage date: the record gives 2011 (Wikidata). LighthouseFriends dates PEI recognition to 1 Nov 2012 and a plaque to 25 Sept 2013; the HistoricPlaces page as read gives no designation date. Not corrected here; a human should check the Canadian Register record.
2. Height: the record's 20.0 m is proposed as 20.6 m (corrections), confirmed by HistoricPlaces (67' 8") and the Society (20.6 m, ground to vane). The record's 20.1 m is the focal height (LighthouseFriends: 20.1 m, 66 ft above high water).
3. Keepers matched by position in the OCR, then confirmed on the page image (scan p.246, printed p.69): the statement row reads 'McDonald, Wm / West Point / Dec. 1, 1875 / 300 00'. The 1875 appointment is therefore from that row as well as the Society's 1875. The line is attached to William MacDonald on the strength of LighthouseFriends and the Society.
4. The 1902 report is the Department's report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1902, printed 1903 (its text says 'the year ended June 30, 1902'). The 39-station passage is on scan p.95, printed p.82 (checked with corpus.py page).
5. Disagreement: automation date, 19 May 1963 (LighthouseFriends) against 29 May 1963 (the Society). Both are stated in the story.
6. Second-hand: Mitchell's 1878 report is read through LighthouseFriends; the 1888 notice is read through the Society, which quotes PEI Agriculture of 21 May 1888; the granddaughter's letter is read through the Society. The original Department reports for 1876-1880 are not in the corpus.
7. Storms: the earlier draft said no wreck was found and left the chapter out. The Society's page does describe wrecks on the West Point reef (Inveresh, 1879; North Star; Roseneath; Ruth Robinson), the grounding of the Nandi in November 1938 and a mid-1940s storm that destroyed the wharf. A chapter has been added from the Society's account only. No newspaper search was run (PEI papers are not in Chronicling America), so the undated wrecks stay undated.
8. The Society's page also carries folklore (a buried-treasure legend, a sea serpent, ghost lights, a bones story). It is left out.
9. The record's characteristic (Iso W 12s) and range (12 nm) come from the Canadian Coast Guard List of Lights; they were not checked here. LighthouseFriends describes the historic 1876 characteristic as one red flash followed by three white flashes every ninety seconds.
10. The lens type is not stated by these sources (LighthouseFriends describes eight lamps and reflectors); the optic is left unstated.
11. Living people: MacIsaac's service ended in 1963 and Frank MacDonald's caretaking after automation; both are named only as LighthouseFriends and the Society print them, in their public role.
